notes:
These are my notes on Isaiah 24. I used the Pulpit Commentary, David Guzik (Enduring Word), Ellicott, Gill, Calvin, Barnes, Matthew Henry, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ligonier and a few others.

**What I couldn't find:** I ran out of searches before reaching any Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal sources, any netbible.org notes, any Orthodox reading, or anything on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Those are left out.

**On part 2:** The pages I read don't say which church tradition each writer belongs to. The real disagreements I found are about end-times schemes and about how far the chapter refers to Israel's history. I've marked those under "Where readers differ" at the relevant verses.

**Overview (chs. 24–27)**
- Ligonier notes that commentators refer to this section as "the little apocalypse." https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/little-apocalypse
- Pulpit: the chapter moves from oracles against single nations (chs. 13–23) to judgment on the whole world, but Israel still has a central place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik: the principles apply to God's judgment in general, but the final fulfilment is the Great Tribulation just before Christ returns. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/
- Modern scholarship: a Gospel Coalition (Themelios) review says scholars who don't think Isaiah wrote the whole book have dated these chapters to the post-exilic period with many dates between the sixth and second centuries bc being suggested. The scholar under review argues that 24:1–20 predicts the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/from-chaos-to-restoration-an-integrative-reading-of-isaiah-24-27/
- Catholic: the Catholic Encyclopedia says that here the Prophet announces for an undetermined future the judgment which shall precede the kingdom of God. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08179b.htm

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: some critics translate "the land" (meaning Israel), but "the earth" fits better because v. 4 mentions "the world" and v. 21 "the kings of the earth." "Empty" is rhetorical: heavy but not total loss of population. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik: the earth won't literally be empty, but it will seem so when more than a third of humanity dies (Rev. 9:15–21). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: God shows "no respect of persons." Isaiah picks social ranks found in almost every nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Ligonier: wealth won't protect anyone; the rich suffer the earth's ruin as much as the poor. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/little-apocalypse
- *Where readers differ:* Guzik argues that since no class escapes, it makes sense for God to remove His people *before* the Tribulation (a pre-tribulation rapture). He presents this against Christians who expect the church to be kept safe while going through it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit: "plundered" means wasted by warring armies, and it compares Jesus' "wars and rumors of wars" (Matt. 24:6–8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Ligonier: "utterly plundered" likely indicates unnatural devastation is in view. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/little-apocalypse

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: the earth fades like a flower. The Hebrew word for "world" always means the whole world. The proud are brought low (compare Isa. 2:11–17). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Ligonier: human sin affects all creation, which groans for release (Gen. 3; Rom. 8). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/little-apocalypse
- Guzik: this is man's fault, not God's. God is separate from His creation and stays unchanged when it fades (he rejects New Age ideas). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**v. 5** (much debated: which "everlasting covenant"?)
- **Covenant with Noah (Gen. 9:16):** Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/isaiah/24-5.htm), Ironside, who says it isn't the Sinai law (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/isaiah-24.html), and Coffman (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-5.html). Matthew Henry says even nations outside the covenant with Abraham benefited from the one with Noah and broke it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_024.cfm
- **The law written on the heart / laws of nature:** Pulpit prefers the covenant built into human nature and conscience (Rom. 2:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html Barnes, following Vitringa, takes it as the immutable laws of justice and right, which are engraven on the conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-5.html
- **Covenant with Israel:** Calvin limits the word to the agreements by which God adopted His people (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-5.html). Matthew Poole points to the covenant with Abraham renewed with Israel (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-5.htm). JFB reads "the land" and sees moral laws, positive statutes and the national covenant (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_024.cfm).
- **Undecided:** Guzik lists five covenants called "everlasting" and says no single one is meant. He applies "changed the ordinance" to softening God's word and moral code today. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: read "a curse" pronounced by God. "Desolate" is better "held guilty." "Burned" means scorched by God's burning anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Pett links the curse to the one in Eden (Gen. 3:17–19). https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/isaiah-24.html

**vv. 7–9**
- Pulpit: even at vintage time nobody celebrates. Men still drink to drown their worries but have no heart to sing, and their troubles make drink taste bitter. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik: no more "partying as usual," comparing "eating and drinking" before the Flood (Matt. 24:38). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/
- Matthew Henry: when worldly mirth stops, the saints' joy does not, because the covenant of grace never fails. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_024.cfm

**vv. 10–12**
- Pulpit: no single city is meant; the word is collective. "Chaos" (*tohu*) rules where there's no order. Houses are barred out of distrust, wine is scarce, and even town gates lie in ruins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- *Different view:* the Themelios review reports a scholar who takes the city as Jerusalem. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/from-chaos-to-restoration-an-integrative-reading-of-isaiah-24-27/

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: only a small, scattered remnant is left, like the few olives and grapes left for gleaners (compare 17:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Ligonier: this probably refers to the faithful remnant who survive and rejoice (vv. 14–16). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/little-apocalypse

**vv. 14–15**
- Pulpit: a faithful remnant praises God in the middle of ruin, largely "from the sea" (the Mediterranean, i.e. the west). In v. 15 the Hebrew reading "in the fires" is uncertain; if kept, it means fiery trials, but the Greek Septuagint suggests "coasts/islands." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik: the singers are people who come to faith during the Tribulation (Rev. 7:9–14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/
- Matthew Henry applies the songs from the ends of the earth to the gospel spreading to distant lands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-22.html

**v. 16**
- **Who is "the Righteous"?** Gill offers three options: the righteous God, Christ the Righteous One, or people made righteous by Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-16.html Ellicott prefers "honour to the righteous," meaning God's people: the word isn't the usual one in praise to God, and "the Righteous One" is never used on its own as a name for God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-16.htm JFB reports Horsley's "the Just One," linking this to the Jews crucifying Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_024.cfm
- **"I am wasting away":** Pulpit says the prophet is pulled back from future glory to present misery, while the ungodly persecute the saints. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html Clarke notes the Latin Vulgate reads "my secret." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-16.html
- Ellicott: the "treacherous" may first mean the Assyrian invaders or Judah's unjust rulers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-16.htm
- Gospel Coalition: Isaiah doesn't gloat over the world's judgment but mourns it. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/isaiah/

**vv. 17–18**
- Pulpit: people are like hunted animals. Jeremiah reuses these words against Moab (Jer. 48:43–44). "Windows of heaven" recalls the Flood: not another flood, but a judgment just as sweeping. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- JFB: a proverb meaning nowhere is safe (compare Amos 5:19). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Isa/Isa_024.cfm
- Guzik: God's judgment can't be escaped. The only way out is to have it satisfied, which happened only at the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**vv. 19–20**
- Pulpit: the physical earth breaks up. "Sways like a shack" is better "like a hammock" (a hanging bed). The earth falls because of human sin and gives way to a new heaven and earth (Rev. 21:1). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik links this to the great earthquake of Rev. 16:18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: the "host of heaven" are fallen spirits, not the good angels who watch over nations (Dan. 10). Compare Eph. 6:12 and Jude 6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html
- Guzik cites Bultema and Wolf: rebel angels locked in the pit until the end of the Millennium (Rev. 20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-24/
- Matthew Henry reads it as proud human rulers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/isaiah/24.htm

**v. 22** (the verse with the widest range of views)
- **Final punishment:** Pulpit says the Hebrew word is the one used for "punish" in v. 21, so being visited for good is "scarcely to be thought of." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html The Cambridge Bible agrees and cites Enoch and Jude. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-22.htm
- **Premillennial:** Gill says punishment comes after the thousand years (Rev. 20). Constable and Chuck Smith also link "many days" to the Millennium. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-22.html
- **Symbolic thousand years:** Coffman, following Hailey, takes the "many days" as the whole time between Christ's first and second comings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-24.html
- **Mercy, tied to history:** Barnes takes it as the 70-year Babylonian exile ending in a visit of deliverance (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-22.html). The Geneva Bible notes say they will be "comforted." JFB sees mercy for the elect and wrath for the hardened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-22.htm
- **Both:** Calvin says the word carries a threat but softens it; the delay is meant to test the faith of the godly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-22.html
- **Neutral:** Ellicott thinks the verb is neutral. He notes that Origen used this verse to argue that all created spirits will finally be restored. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-22.htm

**v. 23**
- **Sun and moon outshone:** Pulpit says they are dimmed by Christ's brightness, not the signs before His coming (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html). The Cambridge Bible says the sun and moon are not being punished (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-23.htm).
- **Sun and moon as symbols:** Barnes reads them as earthly rulers (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-23.html). Benson reads the moon as the Mosaic system and the sun as earthly kingdoms (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-23.htm).
- **Where readers differ, Zion:** Pulpit says only the heavenly Jerusalem can be meant, since the earth is gone (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-24.html). Calvin says "God reigns in Zion" always means mercy and the restoring of the church, fulfilled only in Christ (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/24-23.html). Gill leaves open a literal Jerusalem or the church (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-23.htm). BibleHub's own notes expect a literal Jerusalem capital in Christ's millennial reign (https://biblehub.com/isaiah/24-23.htm).
- **The elders:** Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible point to the 70 elders at Sinai (Exod. 24:9–10). Pulpit compares the 24 elders of Rev. 4:4. Hofmann thinks they are heavenly spirits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/24-23.htm
